Our pick: Poco F9 Ultra (S$1,119 to S$1,699, storage dependent). With memory prices staying elevated, the Poco F9 Ultra becomes a cost-conscious alternative by pairing now-expensive memory with a class-leading chipset. It’s the rare option with 1TB of storage well below S$2,000. If that is your greatest concern, you should start your search with the Poco F9 Ultra before you start weighing its trade-offs, like its camera performance.

...

Your next choice would be the Xiaomi 17 Ultra (S$1,799 for 512GB). Unlike the Poco F9 Ultra, Xiaomi’s main-brand Ultra offers a bang-for-buck approach without compromising key parts of the package (including modest offline storage). It packs comparable (or better) components at a much lower price than its other rivals, and still has reasonable performance in display prowess, camera capabilties, and battery life.

Both Xiaomi’s main and sub-brand options ensure you won’t be short on anything, with the same processor (base version). In particular, Xiaomi’s other specs meet the bare minimum expected of an Ultra.

Your next-lowest-priced choice with a robust hardware and software blend is the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra at S$1,828, but note that it comes with 256GB of storage. For heavy users, this could mean a disciplined approach to keeping apps and media files on the device.

## (Subjective) camera comparison

While we haven’t done a side-by-side camera shootout, we do have some photography tours with these devices that help to showcase the strengths and shortfalls of each Ultra mobile:

These, together with the Vivo X300 Ultra review, makes it clear that producing great photos is mostly a non-issue for their top-tier devices. Choosing a favourite comes down to personal preference, like the onslaught of optional teleconverter kits that Chinese Android phones are happy to offer (at an extra cost).

Of particular note, these are some ways each phone brand tries to go the next mile in imaging prowess:

- OPPO: While it prides itself on accuracy, there’s also plenty of computational photography chops included to make it a versatile shooter for portraits and street photography, letting you get very natural-looking results. Has an optional teleconverter kit if you want to shoot far.
- Poco: We believe it’s a deliberate choice by Xiaomi to make Poco’s imaging performance play second fiddle to its mainline handset; Xiaomi only collaborates with Leica on its mainline mobiles. That said, Poco phones are still capable of delivering usable images if you’re not particular about how your images turn out.
- Samsung: Generally, the all-rounded choice for casual shooters, but it comes with a wealth of expert-level first-party apps hidden away in its own app store, the Galaxy store. It’s still very capable at most optical zoom ranges, with greater emphasis on night-time photography (Nightography).
- Vivo: Also known for its accuracy, while relying on its partnered lenses to convince you it’s the best choice for minimal interference in your images. Also has aggressive computational photography tuning to deliver on photos with bokeh (the focusing blur effect achieved at lower apertures). Also has optical zoom extension through optional teleconverter kits.
- Xiaomi: While it has large sensors for more data capture, its crowning achievement is its use of both the colour and lens tuning seen in proper Leica cameras, which appeal to a crowd that loves dramatised contrast handling, though it’s nowhere near what the real eye sees. Can also support ND filters if you are willing to get a special phone case for them.

...

Our pick: It’s a toss-up between OPPO Find X9 Ultra and Vivo X300 Ultra, owing to their zoom versatility, general consistency across different rear cameras (even ultrawide), and that’s even before we factor in our personal preferences like coloursiation, detail, noise management, and artificial bokeh mastery through computational photography.

That said, the latter makes up for it with amazing, free-of-charge first-party add-ons that you can only find in the Galaxy Store for apps.

title: Google Pixel 11 Pro XL vs Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
text:
The two phones take different approaches to their camera systems. The Galaxy S26 Ultra has a dedicated 3x telephoto camera in addition to its 5x unit, while the Pixel 11 Pro XL makes do with a single 5x telephoto featuring a substantially larger sensor. Their main and ultrawide sensors are more closely matched.

They have a different approach to the front-facing cameras - the Galaxy's selfie camera is wider this year, at 23mm, but the Pixel is in ultrawide territory with its 17mm lens (18mm as per the EXIF), and the sensors are also different - a conventional 12MP on the Galaxy, a Quad Bayer-type one on the Pixel (not that that in itself will make much of a difference).

Main camera photos from the two phones in daylight at 1x carry characteristic traits of each brand's processing, but they're also quite similar too. The Pixel has a grainy detail rendition but it just might have an actual advantage in resolved detail, small as it may be. The Galaxy, meanwhile, has a bit more saturation and warmth in its colors.

Detail at 2x is particularly disappointing from the Pixel, and the Galaxy has a somewhat significant advantage here. That's not to say that it's actually good when compared to the industry-leading efforts; it's just that the Pixel is not very good.

We've seen on previous occasions that the Galaxy's 3x camera is hardly an asset and that gets proven once more in this comparison against the Pixel.

At 3x, the 11 Pro XL shoots composites, merging a center of the frame image sourced from its telephoto with a periphery sourced from the main camera. Sure, there's a relatively visible (not necessarily in-your-face) difference in sharpness between the two areas, but the center where your subject is most likely going to be, is nicely sharp, which you can't say about the Galaxy's images from its dedicated 3x camera.

So despite having a dedicated 3x telephoto camera, the Galaxy doesn't consistently outperform the Pixel at that zoom level. Google's image processing allows it to produce surprisingly competitive 3x photos without a dedicated camera.

The 5x zoom cameras have different takes on detail rendition - the Pixel shots are grittier but likely finer in their presentation, while the Galaxy's sharpening is more heavy-handed. We'd prefer the Pixel take, but it's a small difference, and it just might be subjective.

Oddly enough, the Galaxy takes a relatively convincing victory at 10x, at least in brightly lit outdoor scenes - here its detail is noticeably better defined. Then again, dimmer indoor scenes are inferior on the S26 Ultra.

...

The Pixel is doing just fine at 3x too even though it doesn't have a 3x camera - we'd say it actually outperforms the Galaxy's 3x shooter every ... The Galaxy does liven up a bit in Night mode, but that doesn't really affect the balance all that much.

...

On the selfie front, the Pixel wins for coverage, its 18mm(ish) lens allowing a lot more in the frame. The Galaxy's 23mm lens isn't as wide, but it's arguably wide enough, and the S26 Ultra selfies are higher quality, in good light, and at night. Both feature AF, which can be handy for shots at shorter distances.

...

The Pixel 11 Pro XL remains a compelling camera phone, with excellent image quality across much of its zoom range and particularly wide selfies. Its display also gets substantially brighter in our tests and it's got built-in magnets for wireless charging. But while these are meaningful advantages, the Pixel struggles to match Samsung's broader feature set and raw performance.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra offers considerably more processing power, faster charging, a more versatile video recording experience, and distinctive extras such as Privacy Display, DeX and the integrated S Pen. Its cameras aren't universally better, and the Pixel can sometimes outperform it despite having one fewer rear camera, but the Galaxy offers a more complete package.

With the Galaxy S26 Ultra also available at a lower street price, it's the easier phone to recommend for most buyers. The Pixel 11 Pro XL remains worth considering if you particularly value Google's approach to photography, its wider selfies or the Pixel software experience. Otherwise, the Galaxy is the more convincing all-rounder.

title: Galaxy S26 Ultra vs. OnePlus 15 vs. Pixel 10 Pro XL: The ultimate Android flagship comparison of 2026 - Digital Trends
text:
## Price and availability

Samsung just announced the S26 Ultra — ships March 11, starts at $1,299 for 256GB, goes up to $1,799 for 1TB. Carrier deals with trade-ins can soften that, but the sticker price is what it is.

OnePlus comes in at $899 for the base model, $999 for the 512GB. For context — that’s less than what Google and Samsung charge. It hit US shelves mid-December after getting stuck in FCC approval hell during the government shutdown.

Google launched the Pixel 10 Pro XL back in August at $1,199 for the 256GB variant, and goes up to $1,549 for the 1TB variant. Six months on, you’ll find it discounted pretty regularly if you shop around.

...

All three phones run on 3nm chips. That’s where the common ground ends.

Qualcomm

The S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15 both use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 — though Samsung’s version is tuned specifically for Galaxy hardware. Two prime cores hitting 4.74 GHz, six performance cores at 3.63 GHz, and an Adreno GPU that’s 24% faster than last year’s already-fast silicon.

The NPU is where Samsung pushed hardest though, a 39% jump that handles Galaxy AI’s on-device processing without constantly phoning home to a server. Geekbench scores for the S26 Ultra broke 11,700 multi-core (via Gizmochina), which is a serious number.

The OnePlus 15 runs the same chip with slightly different tuning (two 4.6 GHz prime cores), and benchmarks land comparably close. Day-to-day, you’re not going to feel a meaningful difference between these two — both are fast in a way that currently has no ceiling.

Google

The Pixel 10 Pro XL runs Google’s Tensor G5, built on TSMC’s 3nm node and a genuine step up from the G4. However, the single-core gap between Tensor G5 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 is beyond generational, which shows up in gaming and anything GPU-heavy.

Where Tensor earns its keep is AI — Google’s TPU is optimized specifically for on-device Gemini tasks, and that tight hardware-software integration genuinely shows in how the Pixel handles AI features.

For raw responsiveness and longevity over three or four years, the S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15 are clearly ahead. The Pixel 10 Pro XL is more than capable for daily use, but if gaming or sustained heavy workloads are part of how you use a phone.

## Cameras

Tom Bedford / Digital Trends

On paper and in person as well, the S26 Ultra looks dominant — 200MP main sensor now with a wider f/1.4 aperture (47% more light than last year), a 50MP 5x periscope telephoto that also got a brightness bump, and 8K video recording.

The dual telephoto setup giving you both 3x and 5x optical zoom still makes it the most flexible zoom range of the three, which matters if you shoot a lot of distant subjects. The one thing that’s hard to defend in 2026 is the 10MP 3x telephoto sitting between two high-res powerhouses, and so is the 12MP selfie shooter.

Video-wise, the new APV codec for near-lossless recording and the 360-degree horizon lock on video make this the most capable option for anyone doing serious mobile filmmaking. The phone can also record 4K120 fps videos.

Nadeem Sarwar / Digital Trends

The OnePlus 15’s triple 50MP setup with a 3.5x periscope telephoto was a decent step forward, but dropping Hasselblad tuning in favor of the in-house DetailMax engine was a gamble that hasn’t fully paid off yet. Colors skew warm and punchy — great for social media, less great if you want accuracy.

Low-light is where it starts to fall behind the other two noticeably. While the handset matches the 8K resolution and frame rate (and 4K120 fps video as well), it does have a higher resolution 32MP (f/2.4).

Nirave Gondhia / Digital Trends

The Pixel 10 Pro XL doesn’t try to win on hardware — 50MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP 5x telephoto, same sensors as the Pixel 9 Pro XL. What it does bring is the best image processing of the three, consistently.

Colors come out natural, moving subjects are handled more reliably than competitors, and Google’s AI editing suite — Magic Editor, Best Take, Add Me — is still in a class of its own for post-processing. It also has the sharpest front camera — 42MP — which also has the widest focal length of all (17 mm).

For professional video: S26 Ultra. Consistent daily photography: Pixel 10 Pro XL. Everyday snapshots you want to look good on Instagram: any of them, honestly.

title: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra vs Google Pixel 10 Pro XL | Bandicoot Lab
text:
The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 10 Pro XL are both top-tier Android phones, but they’re pretty different devices. Samsung's phone is the more expensive option at $1,299.99, built around a maximalist camera system with dual telephoto lenses and a focus on raw processing power. Google's Pixel 10 Pro XL at $1,199 leans into computational photography, display quality, and software integration. Both are large-format flagships aimed at buyers who want the best their respective ecosystems offer.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra leads in performance, speaker quality, charging speed, and camera versatility. Its Snapdragon chip delivers substantially more processing headroom. The Pixel 10 Pro XL counters with a brighter, more color-accurate display, better deep zoom consistency, stronger standby battery efficiency, and a microphone that's meaningfully better for calls and voice recording.

...

The Galaxy S26 Ultra runs the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 10 Pro XL uses Google's Tensor G5 with 16GB of RAM.

The gap in performance is large. The S26 Ultra scores 3,685 single-core and 11,198 multi-core in GeekBench 6. The Pixel manages 2,305 single-core and 6,192 multi-core. That's a 60% single-core advantage and an 80% multi-core advantage for Samsung. In practice, this translates to faster app launches, quicker photo processing, and smoother multitasking under heavy load. The Pixel isn't slow in daily use, but the Samsung has headroom the Tensor simply can't match.

GPU performance tells a similar story. The S26 Ultra peaks at 7,802 in Wild Life Extreme versus 3,314 on the Pixel. The Samsung throttles to 49.8% of peak under sustained load, while the Pixel holds 79.4%. The Samsung still delivers higher absolute performance even at its throttled floor (about 3,882 versus 2,632), but it runs hotter doing it, reaching 45°C versus 42°C on the Pixel. For sustained gaming sessions, the Samsung is faster but less consistent.

Browser performance shows the widest relative gap. The S26 Ultra scores 46 in Speedometer versus 15.6 on the Pixel. That's nearly three times the throughput for web-heavy JavaScript tasks. You'll feel this in complex web apps and heavy pages.

...

| | Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (Overall) | Google Pixel 10 Pro XL (Overall) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specifications | | |
| Main | 200MP, f/1.4, 23mm, 1/1.3" | 50MP, f/1.7, 25mm, 1/1.31" |
| Ultrawide | 50MP, f/1.9, 14mm, 1/2.5" | 48MP, f/1.7, 13mm, 1/2.55" |
| Telephoto | 10MP, f/2.4, 67mm, 1/3.94" | 48MP, f/2.8, 113mm, 1/2.55" |
| Telephoto (Long) | 50MP, f/2.9, 111mm, 1/2.52" | — |
| Front | 12MP, f/2.2, 23mm, 1/3.2" | 42MP, f/2.2, 17mm |

Both phones produce sharp, detailed images from their main cameras. The Galaxy S26 Ultra has the more complex system, made up of a main lens, ultrawide, short telephoto, and long telephoto. The Pixel 10 Pro XL carries a main, ultrawide, and single telephoto. In terms of overall sharpness, both deliver high detail at standard focal lengths. The Samsung's main lens is slightly sharper in bright light, while the Pixel edges ahead in low light at 1x. Where they really diverge is zoom behavior and color processing.

At extremely deep zoom levels (80x and beyond), the Pixel 10 Pro XL maintains more consistent sharpness. The Samsung's detail falls off steeply past 60x, relying on aggressive digital processing that produces visible artifacts. The Pixel's output at 80x and 100x holds together better, with less artificial sharpening and more natural texture. For someone who regularly crops or zooms to extreme levels, the Pixel delivers more usable results despite lacking the Samsung's dedicated periscope optics at those distances.

...

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is the more capable phone in raw performance, charging speed, speaker quality, battery endurance during active use, camera versatility, and data transfer. Its dual telephoto system provides optical reach that the Pixel simply doesn't have, and its Snapdragon chip delivers processing power that matters for heavy multitasking, gaming, and demanding apps.

...

The Pixel 10 Pro XL wins on display brightness and color accuracy, standby battery efficiency, deep zoom consistency, front camera sharpness, and microphone quality. If you value an accurate display for photo editing or content work, the Pixel is the better option.

The $100 price difference favors the Pixel though. If processing power, camera system breadth, and speaker quality drive your decision, the Samsung justifies its premium. If display accuracy, deep zoom reliability, and overnight battery preservation matter more, the Pixel delivers those at a lower price with 16GB of RAM to the Samsung's 12GB. Both are excellent phones with distinct strengths. Your priorities should pick the winner.
